frb_ddp.limitation: Not a panel source. Read only by repo_model.effr_history for the pre-SOFR history study (#129): EFFR - IOER from 2008-12-16 to 2018-04-02. EFFR is unsecured overnight lending between depository institutions and GSEs (dominated after 2008 by Federal Home Loan Bank lending to banks that do not earn IOER at the full rate), a different market and a different target from SOFR - IORB. Before 1 March 2016 EFFR was a volume-weighted mean of brokered trades; from that date a volume-weighted median of FR 2420 transactions. The package is the whole release (filetype=zip), read one series at a time by ingest.frb_ddp_series; a date the Board marks ND (holidays) is not a value. The Board's DDP carried a notice on 1 October 2026 that its 'Build Your Package' feature is removed during the week of 9 November 2026 ahead of the DDP's retirement; the full-release package used here may follow.
frb_ddp.provider: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

release_lag.note: EFFR: the H.15 posts at 16:15 ET each business day, carrying the previous business day's rate, so a value is declared available at 16:15 ET one business day after its date. The rate is computed by the New York Fed and published once.

availability_provenance.note: Recorded 2 October 2026 for #115. The H.8 archive's release-date page (https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h8/, fetched 2 October 2026) says the data "are released each Friday, generally at 4:15 p.m., unless Friday is a federal holiday, in which case the data will be released on Thursday, generally at 4:15 p.m." Each archived release page from 25 September 2020 on states "For release at 4:15 p.m. Eastern Time" (51 of the 456 releases from 5 January 2018 to 25 September 2026, all 4:15); the earlier layout states the release date only. 16:15 is after the 16:00 decision instant every published record uses, so a week printed on a Friday is read from the next business day's decision. scripts/extract_h8_first_prints.py refuses a page that states any other time.

release_lag.note: Declared 2 October 2026 for #115, at the measured maximum and not above it. The first print of a week ending Wednesday is released the second Friday after it, 16:15 New York time: nine calendar days for 443 of the 456 weeks from 2017-12-27 to 2026-09-16 in the tracked extract, eight for the nine weeks released on a Thursday before a Friday holiday, and twelve for four: the weeks ending 2020-12-09 (released Monday 2020-12-21), 2020-12-16 (Monday 2020-12-28), 2021-06-09 (Monday 2021-06-21, the first Juneteenth) and 2025-12-17 (Monday 2025-12-29). Twelve is that worst case, so every value is declared public no earlier than it was; an ordinary week is then read three days later than it could have been, which is staleness on the safe side, not leakage. The extract script refuses a week first printed later than this declaration, so a longer delay in a future release stops the extract rather than leaking. The values are first prints, which no later release changes in the extract.

DFF.note: Declared 15 September 2026. FIVE IS ELEONORA'S DECISION OF 15 SEPTEMBER 2026 AND NOT A DERIVATION: the tracked vintages measure four, and the fifth day is a deliberate cushion above what is measured, taken in the shape IORB's number was taken in. DFF is the H.15's effective federal funds rate (FRED release rid=18), calendar-daily: a value is dated to the day it describes and first published the next morning the desk publishes, which is not the next calendar day when that day is a weekend or a holiday. WHERE THE FOUR COMES FROM, precisely: consecutive-day ALFRED vintages under tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-dff-first-print/ date each observation's first appearance exactly, and the 2026-09-07 vintage (Labor Day Monday) ends at 2026-09-03 while the 2026-09-08 vintage first carries 2026-09-04, 2026-09-05, 2026-09-06 and 2026-09-07 -- so Friday 2026-09-04's value first appears on Tuesday 2026-09-08, four calendar days. The same fixtures show three days across an ordinary weekend (2026-08-31 first carries 2026-08-28) and one day within a week. FOUR IS A FLOOR, NOT A PROVEN WORST CASE: it is the longest gap one Labor Day weekend produced in the tracked vintages, and an unscheduled closure -- a market-wide holiday, a weather closure, a day of national mourning appended to a holiday weekend -- could exceed it. The fifth day is for exactly that. THE FIFTH DAY IS FREE: over the fields the published funding record docs/runs/exceedance_gbm_cross_conformal_funding_mh61.json declares, at its 16:00 decision time, a run that also reads DFF purges 6 days with DFF at four and 6 with DFF at five -- the same 6 the nine features already cost -- while DFF at six would purge 7. The headroom was taken where it costs nothing and stopped before it costs a day of history. The number is held at both ends by test_registry.DffFirstPrintRecordTests, which asserts this entry equals the measured floor plus its named HEADROOM_DAYS, so neither a retreat to four nor a drift to six can pass.
DFF.revision_evidence: Eight ALFRED vintages of DFF, fetched 15 September 2026 and tracked under tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-dff/ (2020-01-15, 2023-06-30, 2026-09-01) and tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-dff-first-print/ (2020-03-20, 2026-08-30, 2026-08-31, 2026-09-07, 2026-09-08), carry no restatement of any value. `python3 scripts/alfred_vintages.py tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-dff/*.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-dff-first-print/*.csv` re-runs the comparison over all 28 pairs and exits 1 if an observation is ever restated; it exits 0 today, identical on every shared observation -- 23939 of 23939 between 2020-01-15 and each later vintage back to 1954-07-01, 25201 of 25201 between 2023-06-30 and 2026-09-01, and 24004 of 24004 between the 2020-03-20 vintage and every later one, which is the first print of the 2020-03-16 cut to 0.25 and the 0.20 that followed. Unlike WRESBAL there is no units rescale in any pair, and unlike RRPONTSYD there is no differing observation at all, so neither the constant-ratio case nor the restatement case arises. The rate is computed by the New York Fed from the prior day's transactions and published once; latest vintage therefore stands in for a point-in-time record on this field.

IOER.note: Added 8 September 2026 so the administered leg of SOFR - IORB can be priced before 2021-07-29. Without it the funding panel begins in July 2021 and contains neither September 2019 nor March 2020. The splice is declared in contract.FEATURE_FIELDS and guarded by build_daily_panel rule 7, which raises if IOER and IORB ever report the same reference date. Vintage-verified 10 September 2026 from the user's fetch; until then the never-revised claim rested on the administrative argument alone. Priced at zero days since docs/decisions/iorb-availability.md: IOER for a date is announced, with its effective date, before that date.
IOER.revision_evidence: Three ALFRED vintages of IOER -- 2019-01-02, 2021-07-27 and 2024-09-24, tracked under tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-ioer/ -- agree on every overlapping observation: 3739 identical values from 2008-10-09 to 2019-01-03 across a five-year vintage gap, and 4676 identical values from 2008-10-09 to 2021-07-28 between the last live vintage and the latest. No observation has been restated; `python3 scripts/alfred_vintages.py tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-ioer/*.csv` re-runs the comparison and exits 1 if one ever is. The rate was set by the Board of Governors and announced ahead of its effective date, which the vintages show: the 2019-01-02 vintage already carries 2019-01-03 and the 2021-07-27 vintage carries 2021-07-28, the final observation. The value for a date is therefore public before that date, which is the zero-day lag of docs/decisions/iorb-availability.md. IOER ends 2021-07-28 and IORB begins 2021-07-29, abutting with no overlap and no gap.

IORB.note: IORB for a date is announced, with its effective date, in the FOMC implementation note before that date. The zero-day lag is decided in docs/decisions/iorb-availability.md, which supersedes the one-day lag declared 8 September 2026. The 16:15 instant still prices the value later than the announcement shows it was known.
IORB.revision_evidence: Three ALFRED vintages of IORB -- 2024-09-01, 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-04 -- agree on every overlapping observation: 1130 identical values from 2021-07-29 to 2024-08-31 across a two-year vintage gap, and 1864 identical values from 2021-07-29 to 2026-09-04. No observation has been restated. The rate is administered by the Board of Governors and announced in advance of its effective date, which the vintages themselves show: the 2026-09-03 vintage already carries observations dated 2026-09-04, and the 2026-09-04 vintage carries through 2026-09-08, as the zero-day lag of docs/decisions/iorb-availability.md requires. Latest vintage is therefore point-in-time for this field and for no other field of this source.

WLRRAOL.note: Declared 16 September 2026. WHAT THIS IS: the H.4.1's reverse-repurchase-agreements line, "Liabilities and Capital: Liabilities: Reverse Repurchase Agreements: Others: Wednesday Level" (FRED release rid=20, Table 1) -- the Wednesday OUTSTANDING level of the overnight reverse repo facility. It is NOT the Desk's operational ON RRP series RRPONTSYD (FRED rid=379, Temporary Open Market Operations), which stays refused, and it is not WLRRAL, the H.4.1's total reverse-repo line, which also carries the foreign official and international pool (WLRRAFOIAL). Declaring this field builds no column: the on_rrp column still maps to RRPONTSYD in contract.py, which is human-owned. WHY FIVE DAYS: the H.4.1 is published Thursdays, generally at 16:30 New York time, for the week ending the previous Wednesday, and the observation dates are those Wednesdays, so an ordinary week is one calendar day. But the Board's own rule is that publication "may be shifted to the next business day when the regular publication date falls on a federal holiday", and the shift is measured rather than hypothetical: the week ending Wednesday 2020-12-23 is absent from the 2020-12-24 and 2020-12-27 ALFRED vintages of WLRRAOL and first carried by the 2020-12-28 one -- five calendar days -- exactly as for WRESBAL, under tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-h41-first-print/. The Board's archive agrees: releases/h41/20201228/ exists, "Release Date: December 28, 2020", for the week ended December 23, and releases/h41/20201224/ is a 404; its Wednesday-level "Reverse repurchase agreements ... Others" line for that week is 857, which is this series' 2020-12-23 value to the million (re-fetched 16 September 2026). Five is that measured floor exactly and not a cushion above it, the same number WRESBAL and WTREGEN carry, so the three lines of one release carry one lag. Five is a floor from the tracked vintages, not a worst case -- the stated rule allows longer if a Thursday closure meets a longer run of holidays. THE DECISION: job 651 priced this declaration on the merged tree in memory without declaring it, and Eleonora decided on 16 September 2026 to build it, at five days. FIVE IS FREE AND SIX IS NOT: over the eleven (source, field) pairs the published funding record docs/runs/exceedance_gbm_cross_conformal_funding_mh61.json declares in derived.fields, at its 16:00 decision time, the purge is 6 without WLRRAOL, 6 with WLRRAOL at any lag from 1 to 5, and 7 at six -- six would cost a day of history. VALUE UNIT: MILLIONS of US dollars in every tracked vintage; unlike WRESBAL and WTREGEN this line was never served in billions, so no rescale separates its vintages. That is recorded in prose because the registry's `unit` key is the unit of the release lag, not of the value. The number is held at both ends by test_registry.WlrraolFirstPrintRecordTests, which asserts this entry equals the first-print floor computed from the tracked vintages and that it leaves the published funding record's purge where it was while a day more would not.
WLRRAOL.revision_evidence: Ten ALFRED vintages of WLRRAOL -- 2019-09-19, 2020-01-02, 2020-03-26, 2020-11-27, 2021-07-29, 2024-09-26, 2026-09-03, 2026-09-08, 2026-09-09 and 2026-09-10, tracked under tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/ -- carry no restatement of any value. `python3 scripts/alfred_vintages.py tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2019-09-19.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2020-01-02.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2020-03-26.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2020-11-27.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2021-07-29.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2024-09-26.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2026-09-03.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2026-09-08.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2026-09-09.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wlrraol/WLRRAOL_2026-09-10.csv` re-runs the comparison over all 45 pairs and exits 1 if an observation is ever restated; it exits 0 today (re-run 16 September 2026), identical on every shared observation -- 875 of 875 from 2002-12-18 between the 2019-09-19 vintage and every later one, and 1137 of 1137 between 2024-09-26 and each 2026 vintage. Unlike WRESBAL there is no units rescale in any pair, and unlike RRPONTSYD there is no differing observation at all: RRPONTSYD was restated on 2020-02-19 and 2020-11-18, two-operation days on which FRED alternated between the sum and one leg, so RRPONTSYD remains refused.

WRESBAL.note: Declared 14 September 2026, when the never-revised claim was measured rather than argued; the lag was corrected from one day to five on 15 September 2026, and the never-revised claim is unaffected. The H.4.1 is published Thursdays, generally at 16:30 New York time, for the week ending the previous Wednesday, and the observation dates are those Wednesdays, so an ordinary week is one calendar day. But the Board's own rule is that publication "may be shifted to the next business day when the regular publication date falls on a federal holiday", and the shift is measured rather than hypothetical: the week ending Wednesday 2020-12-23 is absent from the 2020-12-24 and 2020-12-27 ALFRED vintages and first carried by the 2020-12-28 one -- five calendar days -- for WRESBAL exactly as for WLRRAOL, the two lines of the same release, under tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-h41-first-print/. The Board's archive agrees: releases/h41/20201228/ exists, "Release Date: December 28, 2020", for the week ended December 23, and releases/h41/20201224/ is a 404. Its "Reserve balances with Federal Reserve Banks" line for that week is 3143041, which is this series' 2020-12-23 value to the million. Five is that measured floor exactly and not a cushion above it; the number is Eleonora's decision of 15 September 2026, taken at the floor and not above it. Five rather than six because six would cost a day of history: over the fields the published funding record declares, at its 16:00 decision time, the purge is 6 at every lag from 1 to 5 and 7 at six. Five is a floor from the tracked vintages, not a worst case -- the stated rule allows longer if a Thursday closure meets a longer run of holidays. VALUE UNIT: the series is served in MILLIONS of US dollars as of the 2026 vintage, having been served in billions through the 2024 vintage. That is recorded in prose because the registry's `unit` key is the unit of the release lag, not of the value; a value-unit key would be a change to contract.py, which is human-owned and was not made for this.
WRESBAL.revision_evidence: Four ALFRED vintages of WRESBAL -- 2019-09-16, 2021-07-27, 2024-09-24 and 2026-09-12, tracked under tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wresbal/ -- carry no restatement of any value. `python3 scripts/alfred_vintages.py tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wresbal/WRESBAL_2019-09-16.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wresbal/WRESBAL_2021-07-27.csv tests/fixtures/snapshots/alfred-wresbal/WRESBAL_2024-09-24.csv` re-runs the comparison across the three pre-rescale vintages and exits 1 if an observation is ever restated; it exits 0 today, on every observation the three share back to the 1980s. The 2026-09-12 vintage differs from all three, and differs on EVERY shared observation by EXACTLY a factor of one thousand -- 874, 971 and 1136 observations respectively, without exception -- which is a units rescale from billions to millions, not a revision. That classification is what separates this field from RRPONTSYD, whose differences are not a constant ratio: it was restated on 2020-02-19 from 5.149 to 0.095, and on 2020-11-18 from 0.103 to 0.000 and back to 0.103, so RRPONTSYD remains refused.

availability_provenance.note: The publication mechanic is a human-supplied reading of the New York Fed's methodology, recorded 12 September 2026; no code here fetches that page. What was fetched the same day, through repo_model.ingest.fetch_nyfed_reference_rate, is the rate data itself: snapshots pinned in the gitignored data/raw by sha256 -- nyfed_tgcr rate cdaf52e9638cc977 volume 5e87d2b7aa4815c0, nyfed_bgcr rate b1cd7969ac8f1bd2 volume afcffe123cf95f16. It replaces a note that cited only 'the conservative finalized availability time used uniformly by the adapter'.
availability_provenance.publication: New York Fed Overnight Reference Rates methodology: TGCR, BGCR and SOFR are calculated from the prior business day's transactions and published together at about 08:00 ET on the next business day, with a contingent revision window that closes at 14:30 ET. 15:00 ET on the next business day is therefore the conservative finalized availability instant, after the revision window rather than at the first print.

nyfed_bgcr.limitation: Publication occurs after the effective date; targets and features must respect that lag.
nyfed_bgcr.provider: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

release_lag.note: BGCR is first published on the next business day; 15:00 ET is the conservative finalized availability time used uniformly by the adapter.

nyfed_bgcr.reviewed_note: Structural-zero semantics have not yet been reviewed against the New York Fed response schema; the empty declaration is not a finding.

availability_provenance.note: Declared 2 October 2026 for directive #98. The publication time is declared conservatively rather than measured: no code here fetches the New York Fed's methodology page, and one retrieval of the rate data bounds the lag without measuring it. The instant is the one the secured rates carry, so EFFR and SOFR for a day are read at the same panel row. At this project's 16:00 decision time any declared instant from the morning print up to 16:00 on the next business day reads the same row, so the 15:00 instant costs no history against the 09:00 first print. The tracked snapshot, retrieved through repo_model.ingest.fetch_nyfed_effr one calendar year per request, carries an empty revisionIndicator on every record from 2018-01-02 to 2026-09-30.
availability_provenance.publication: New York Fed effective federal funds rate: calculated from the prior business day's FR 2420 overnight federal funds transactions and published at about 09:00 ET on the next business day. 15:00 ET on the next business day is declared as the conservative availability instant, after any same-morning correction, matching the instant the New York Fed's secured reference rates carry here.

nyfed_effr.limitation: Publication occurs after the effective date; targets and features must respect that lag. Fetched from the New York Fed as published, not from FRED's DFF copy of the same rate.
nyfed_effr.provider: Federal Reserve Bank of New York

release_lag.note: EFFR is first published at about 09:00 ET on the next business day; 15:00 ET that day is the conservative availability time, the one the secured reference rates carry.

nyfed_effr.reviewed_note: Structural-zero semantics have not yet been reviewed against the New York Fed response schema; the empty declaration is not a finding.

availability_provenance.note: Read on the human side and recorded 12 September 2026; it is a human-supplied reading and not something any code here fetched. The clause this replaces said the project has no network route to the New York Fed, which is no longer true -- a job running natively on the user's machine does reach it, and the adapter added in A34 fetches this source from there. What has not changed is the part the provenance rests on: no code reads the release schedule this note cites, so the availability claim is still a human reading and the snapshot still cannot corroborate it. The snapshot cannot corroborate it -- the tracked fixture's manifest records a url and a retrieved_at, but one download bounds the lag rather than measuring it -- which is why the release_lag note already rests the six-business-day gap on the schedule rather than on the file. This object makes the publication claim behind the early available_time machine-readable, as registry.check_availability_provenance requires of any instant earlier than the end-of-day convention.

identities.eras_note: The identity is evaluated era by era because the source's vocabulary has a history and its data does not have a hole. Declared over the current thirteen terms alone it can be evaluated on 243 of the tracked extract's 700 weekly as-of dates and is not_evaluable on the other 457. The alternative that is refused rather than merely not chosen is one identity over the union of all fifteen terms: on a date in an early era the later era's terms are absent, so the union is not_evaluable everywhere -- and read an absent term as 0.0 to make the sum close and it holds everywhere instead, which turns an absence into a measured value.

identities.tolerance_note: Exact, and absolute-only for the same reason shareholder_flows_reconcile is: the total is a re-summation of its era's terms in the same export, not two independently measured quantities that happen to agree. On the tracked fixture at 2026-08-26 the residual is 5.7e-14 USD billions, which is the double-precision cost of dividing fourteen integers by 1000 and adding thirteen of them, and a bound of a millionth of a billion is the statement that nothing but that is tolerated. The thirteen terms are named one by one and never globbed, and so are the eleven and the twelve of the two earlier eras -- see eras and eras_note above. The globs PDPOSGSC-* and PDPOSTIPS-* also match the C-suffixed series in the same buckets -- PDPOSGSC-L2C and its siblings -- and summing those in gives 492637 rather than 477607 millions at that date, so a glob does not merely risk overshooting the total, it does overshoot it on the only date this repository can check.

A value of '*' marks a figure the New York Fed withheld for confidentiality. It yields no observation -- never 0.0, and never a parse failure -- and a '*' in a declared series is recorded in the build's quality report under absent_cells with reason suppressed, dated by its row's As Of Date. That record is what distinguishes a suppression from a series the export simply does not contain, which is no cell and is not recorded. PDPOSGST-TOT's identity records the same week: a week with a suppressed term evaluates to not_evaluable, naming the term, rather than to violated. The series is a panel column: contract.FEATURE_FIELDS maps dealer_treasury_position to PDPOSGST-TOT, so a build that carries the column depends on this source and a violated identity in it stops that build. Only the fifteen fields declared above are read -- fourteen current ones and PDPOSGSC-G11, the over-eleven-year bucket retired in 2022, which is declared so the identity's earlier eras have their own components to be checked against and which appears in no current export; every other series in the export is ignored rather than parsed, so a suppression or a malformed value in one of them is invisible to this adapter.

release_lag.note: The lag rests on the New York Fed's published Primary Dealer Statistics release schedule and not on the snapshot, which cannot corroborate it: the tracked fixture's manifest records the url it was downloaded from, https://markets.newyorkfed.org/api/pd/get/all/timeseries.csv, and the retrieved_at of that download, 2026-09-14T00:31:00.991705+00:00, but one download shows only that the latest as-of date it carries, 2026-09-02, had been published by then -- a bound on the lag and not a measurement of it. Six business days from a Wednesday as-of date is the Thursday of the following week -- 2026-08-26 becomes available 2026-09-03 -- which is the calendar-week-plus-a-day gap the documented schedule describes. The directive that queued this adapter asked for 'calendar days 8' and a worst case of 9, and neither is expressible: src/repo_model/contract.py pins UNIT_FOR_BASIS['ref_date'] to 'business_days', so a calendar_days count on this basis is refused outright, and validate_release_lag requires worst_case_calendar_days to be at least days + 5, which puts the smallest admissible bound at 11 rather than 9. Six business days and eight calendar days name the same Thursday on a week with no holiday, and the business-day form is the one that shifts to Friday when one intervenes, which is what the directive's '(Thursday-holiday shift)' worst case describes. contract.py is human-owned, so both refusals are recorded here rather than worked around; 11 is conservative against 9 in the direction splits.py establishes as safe.

eras.note: Original Form N-MFP, from the first monthly filing in November 2010. The universe falls from 730 series to 546 across the era.
Form N-MFP2, the 2014 money-market-fund reform amendments. The structural 2a-7 changes that consolidated the industry took effect 14 October 2016, inside this era rather than at its start.

Form N-MFP3, the 2023 amendments. Bounded at the newest month the declared archive set carries, for the same reason NMFP_INVESTMENT_CATEGORY_ERAS bounds its last era: a month nobody has observed has no calibrated floor, and refusing it is the fail-closed reading.

cross_section.note: Each bulk extract covers a filing window and carries one dominant monthly cross-section plus amendment and straggler filings for adjacent months, and the stragglers are not a universe. The floor counts distinct SERIESID and never a value total, because the values are what the floor exists to make trustworthy. A ref_date below its era's floor is excluded from the panel and recorded in the quality report, with the SUBMISSIONTYPE mix of its submissions alongside as a corroborating record that is never a filter. The floor is per era because one absolute cannot hold across a universe that changes size: the single floor of 200 this replaced was 27 percent of the 2010 universe and 65 percent of the 2024 one. It is an absolute count per era rather than a fraction of a trailing median because the trailing median is itself computed from straggler months -- on the 2026-07 extract the straggler counts have a median of 4, so a quarter-of-median rule would set the floor at 1 and admit the 1-series cross-section it was written to reject. Each era's floor is 60 percent of the smallest complete month observed inside it, the same proportion the original single floor used, and observed_minimum_entities and observed_complete_months state what it was measured over. Those counts were derived on 9 September 2026 from the 97 archives on disk, on assembled monthly cross-sections rather than report dates: the earlier counts in this note were measured per REPORTDATE and understated every split month by whichever half they missed -- 2013-06 files 159 series on the 28th and 473 on the 30th, 632 assembled, against 634 and 629 in the adjacent months. 54 of the 189 months are split. The era BOUNDARIES are declared from the Form N-MFP version, which is a dated published fact about who files and on what schedule. They are deliberately not derived from the counts, because a floor that infers its own eras from the data it judges is calibrated against the evidence that is supposed to check it. They should not be read as steps in the size of the universe, and the counts say they are not: the universe declines smoothly and almost monotonically from 730 to 307 with no discontinuity at either boundary. 2016-03 to 2016-04 falls 546 to 529, the third largest month-over-month fall of 188 and smaller than 2013-02 to 2013-03; 2024-05 to 2024-06 does not fall at all, 323 to 323, ranking 123rd. These bounds coincide with NMFP_INVESTMENT_CATEGORY_ERAS because both follow the form version, not because either was fitted to the other; nothing asserts they must stay equal, and a form version that rewrites the categories without moving the universe is exactly the case where they should be allowed to diverge. A ref_date in no declared era is refused and named, never admitted on the nearest era's floor.

identities.name: series_assets_reconcile_to_liabilities_and_net_assets
identities.tolerance_note: An absolute bound, and after calibration it stays one. The deferral this note used to carry -- a relative bound withheld 'until at least three cross-sections are admitted' -- has expired, and the answer it was waiting for is no. Derived over the 124 admitted cross-sections on which every declared term is observed; 65 further admitted cross-sections are not evaluable at all, being the n_mfp1 era, which does not report this balance sheet. Scale, taken as the larger side of the identity the way the verdict takes it, runs 3178 to 9254 USD billions across those 124 -- a factor of 2.9. The case this note used to make for a relative bound cited three orders of magnitude of scale, and that population no longer exists: the per-era coverage floor refuses the small cross-sections that made the case, and monthly assembly merged the split month-ends that halved the rest. Over a 2.9x range a relative bound and an absolute one are nearly the same bound. Measured rather than argued: normalising the residual by scale moves its dispersion from 0.764 to 0.745 decades and leaves its rank correlation with scale at +0.05. Scale explains almost none of the spread, so a relative_ppm has almost nothing to correct. What the spread is instead: the residual is 0.92 USD billions at the median, 10.34 at the 95th percentile and 35.14 at its worst, which in parts per million of scale is 171, 1312 and 6395. This bound admits 44 of the 124 and refuses 80. Two facts sit under that and neither is a bound problem. First, from 2024-06 to 2026-02 -- 21 consecutive months, beginning exactly at the declared n_mfp2 to n_mfp3 boundary and resolving after it -- the identity breaks one-sidedly, assets exceeding liabilities plus net assets in all 21, by 1035 ppm and 8.57 USD billions at the median and 2597 ppm at its worst. A bound sized to admit that would be sized to admit a defect that starts and stops on a form-version boundary. Second, outside that window the residual is two-sided -- assets larger on 37 of 103 -- and still exceeds this bound on 59 of 103, at a median of 0.66 USD billions. So the bound is tight for the well-behaved regime too, but tight in absolute terms at every scale, which is not what a relative_ppm corrects. The tolerance is therefore left where it was: this is an ingestion check that currently fails on a majority of the population it checks, and widening it would turn it into a description of that population. The schema accepts relative_ppm alongside absolute and src/repo_model/contract.py resolves the pair as max(absolute, relative_ppm * 1e-6 * scale); the mechanism is present and exercised. What is absent is a reason to use it here. The 2024-06 to 2026-02 break is a finding against the ingestion or the filings and is not this number's to absorb.

sec_nmfp.limitation: As-filed data may contain reporting errors and becomes available after month-end. Refusal is per table. A table the archive does not carry costs exactly the panel fields it supplies, which then have no observation from that archive -- absent, never zero -- and the archive is read for everything else; metadata/sec_nmfp_archives.json records this per archive as a refusals entry of kind absent_fields naming those fields. A table that is present with a column the adapter reads under a changed name refuses the whole archive (kind unreadable), because a renamed column reaches the parser as an absent value and yields a silently partial series that still satisfies the balance-sheet identity; such an archive contributes no observations and is not placed under data/raw/. NMFP_SUBMISSION.tsv is the one table whose absence is unreadable rather than a cost in fields, because without it no row can be attributed to a series or a report date. Schema compatibility across the published history was diffed archive by archive on 7 September 2026: of 97 declared archives, all 97 are read; the 71 filed before 2024-06-10 carry no NMFP_DLYSHAREHOLDERFLOWREPORT.tsv, because daily shareholder-flow reporting began with Form N-MFP3, so mmf_gross_subscriptions, mmf_gross_redemptions and mmf_net_flow have no observation for those filing windows. Header compatibility is not value compatibility: every column this adapter reads is present under the same name back to 2010q4, but INVESTMENTCATEGORY is a categorical the adapter matches on by value and its vocabulary was rewritten at the 2016-04 report month (Treasury Debt to U.S. Treasury Debt, and every other label with it) and again at 2024-06 (U.S. Government Agency Debt split into coupon-paying and no-coupon variants; the Other Repurchase Agreement label reworded). The accepted and deliberately excluded category strings are therefore declared per era in NMFP_INVESTMENT_CATEGORY_ERAS, enumerated from all 97 archives rather than from documentation. A category string an era does not declare raises rather than matching nothing, and a report month in no declared era loses mmf_treasury_holdings, mmf_repo_holdings and mmf_on_rrp for that cross-section and nothing else. The last era is bounded by the newest report month the declared archive set carries, because the vocabulary is still moving. The declared column set is per table and lives in the adapter, not here: NMFP_REQUIRED_COLUMNS in src/repo_model/ingest.py is derived from the same balance-field and flow-field mappings the parser reads, and a header missing any of that set refuses the table before a row is parsed, so this registry carries no copy of the column names for the parser to drift away from. Values are parsed by _nmfp_number, which strips commas as thousands separators before float(), so an extract written with a decimal comma parses silently and wrong by a power of ten -- 1234,5 reads as 12345.0 and 1234,56 as 123456.0, while a European 1.234,56 reads as 1.23456 -- and that behaviour is recorded here rather than fixed, because a locale-sniffing heuristic would be a silent behaviour change calibrated on data nobody has seen, and a differently-formatted extract should fail loudly rather than parse plausibly.

release_lag.note: The bulk extract is a monthly compilation of as-filed submissions; rows inherit the immutable extract retrieval timestamp rather than the filing deadline or report date.

sec_nmfp.reviewed_note: Reviewed for mmf_on_rrp alone, the one field whose absence the archive made reviewable (docs/DATA_QUALITY_DECISIONS.md, 'the ON RRP leg'). The other ten fields declare no structural zero and that is not a finding that they have none: the three shareholder-flow fields have no observation before Form N-MFP3 because the table did not exist, which metadata/sec_nmfp_archives.json records as absent_fields refusals -- an absence with a reason, not a zero.

structural_zeros.when: mmf_on_rrp is the Fund's reverse repo lent to the Federal Reserve through the overnight reverse repurchase facility, which opened in September 2013; a report month through 2013-08 that carries no mmf_on_rrp row held none, because there was no facility to lend to. The declaration covers absent cross-sections only: the two pre-facility months the archive does report (2011-03-31, 1.2 USD billions; 2012-11-30, 0.8) stay observations, and are not explained here. It is bounded at 2013-08-31 so that it cannot reach 2026-07-31, the one month after the facility opened with no row, which stays an undeclared absence.

treasury_auctions.limitation: treasury_settlement is one aggregate: the announced offering amounts of every auction sharing an issue_date, summed and converted to USD billions. All security types are aggregated, so tenor structure is not represented. SOMA add-ons are not in it, which this note said the opposite of until 10 September 2026: offering_amt is the announced public offering, and the Federal Reserve's rollover bids are noncompetitive tenders treated as add-ons to the announced auction size, with Treasury increasing the total issue by the SOMA award (Federal Reserve Bank of New York, 'FAQs: Treasury Rollovers'). The Fed's leg is therefore absent from this series, not mixed into it. Both omissions matter to a repo model specifically. Bill and coupon settlements have different collateral and reserve-drain profiles, and bill supply is close to the centre of the 2018-19 episode this project exists to model. Fed SOMA add-ons do not drain private cash, so leaving them out is right for the private-sector drain; what is missing is the Fed's leg as its own series, which src/repo_model/contract.py now defines as a component outside the aggregate. security_type, security_term and soma_accepted are all present in the snapshot, and as of 10 September 2026 the adapter reads security_type and soma_accepted: treasury_settlement_bill and treasury_settlement_coupon sum offering_amt by Treasury's own bills-versus-coupons split and are the two terms of the declared identity, while treasury_settlement_soma sums soma_accepted and sits outside it. Splitting the series needed no new download. A settlement date with no auction of a kind carries no observation for that leg rather than a zero, and a settlement date any of whose auctions had not been held at retrieval -- Fiscal Data writes an unavailable result as the string 'null' -- carries no treasury_settlement_soma at all, rather than a zero or the partial sum of its held siblings. Those two sentences describe the adapter's observations, not the panel columns, which differ by one rule since 11 September 2026 (src/repo_model/data.py, build_daily_panel rule 8): a date on the panel's grid, inside a snapshot's coverage from its first settlement date to its retrieval date, reads 0.0 for a leg with no observation and for the aggregate on a date with no auction at all, while treasury_settlement_soma reads 0.0 only on a date with no settlement of any kind, so a withheld result stays a hole.This note replaces one that said announcement and result vintages must be separated to avoid using auction outcomes too early. That risk is avoided by construction and was never the live one, but the reason this note gave for it was wrong until 10 September 2026, when the snapshot was first read: the note said record_date drives available_at and is part of vintage_id, so an announced but unsettled auction is visible from its publication date and not before. record_date equals issue_date on all 3562 rows of the tracked snapshot and is greater than or equal to auction_date on all of them, so it is the settlement date, not a publication date, and an auction becomes visible on the day it settles rather than on the day it was announced. That is more conservative than the sentence claimed and is not a leak, but it is a different fact, and a lag argued from the wrong one is not argued. The adapter reads offering_amt and soma_accepted, and never total_accepted, high_yield or bid_to_cover; soma_accepted is an auction result, and it is admitted only where record_date does not precede its auction_date, which on this snapshot is everywhere. A limitation describing a risk the adapter avoids absolutely, while silent on the one it creates, reads as vigilance.
treasury_auctions.provider: U.S. Department of the Treasury Fiscal Data

release_lag.note: record_date is the settlement date on this dataset, not a publication date: it equals issue_date on every row of the tracked snapshot and never precedes auction_date. Dating availability from it is therefore conservative by days rather than exact, and end-of-day availability additionally avoids assuming an intraday time. Corrected 10 September 2026; the previous note asserted Fiscal Data's generic definition of record_date as a publication date, which this dataset does not follow.

treasury_auctions.reviewed_note: Structural-zero semantics have not yet been reviewed against the Treasury auction data dictionary; the empty declaration is not a finding.

scheduled_availability.evidence: The tracked snapshot tests/fixtures/snapshots/funding_inputs/treasury_auctions/20260914T051023Z_722359ea9bc7.json (Fiscal Data auctions_query, retrieved 2026-09-14T05:10:23Z) carries auction_date, issue_date and closing_time_comp for each of its 3828 auctions. On every auction settling on or after the published panel's first date, 2018-04-03, auction_date is strictly before issue_date; three cash management bills earlier in the snapshot were auctioned and settled on the same day (2017-09-08, 2017-12-08, 2018-01-19), so the claim is established for the panel's span and not as a rule of Treasury's. A same-day cash management bill inside the panel would make it false for that day, and ingest.check_settlement_schedule, run by every build (repo_model.cli build), refuses the build when any auction settling inside the panel window closed later than 15:00 New York time on the panel day before its settlement, a same-day settlement included. On the panel's own dates the auction falls at least one panel day before settlement (36 auctions exactly one panel day before, all closing at or before 13:00), and no auction closed for competitive bids later than 14:30 (two bill auctions on 2025-07-07; the rest at 10:00, 11:00, 11:30 or 13:00). tests/test_asof.py::DeclarationTests re-checks this on the tracked snapshot. offering_amt is fixed at the auction announcement, before the auction; soma_accepted is fixed by the auction result. Treasury's results-publication time, checked 1 October 2026 (#59): Treasury's auction procedure states no clock time, only that results are published on TreasuryDirect after the auction concludes (31 CFR 356.23(a); see the note). The 15:00 instant therefore rests on the auction data alone: it leaves 30 minutes after the latest close in the snapshot and two hours after the latest close of any auction settling the next panel day.
scheduled_availability.note: Approved by Eleonora on 30 September 2026 (docs/decisions/information-set.md, rule 2): settlements are scheduled inputs dated from the auction results time. The value for settlement date d is declared public at 15:00 New York time on the panel day before d. That instant rests on the auction data (the closing times and auction dates recorded in the snapshot), not on a published results-publication time, because Treasury publishes none. Its auction procedure, the Uniform Offering Circular, says only: "After the conclusion of the auction, we will make the auction results available on our website at http://www.treasurydirect.gov." (31 CFR 356.23(a), https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/section-356.23, read 1 October 2026, #59). TreasuryDirect's 'How auctions work' page (https://www.treasurydirect.gov/auctions/how-auctions-work/) gives one clock time, for TreasuryDirect account holders only: 'you can see the results of your bid after 5 PM Eastern time on auction day'; it gives none for the public results. The 15:00 instant precedes the 16:00 decision time every published run uses, and every build refuses an auction that contradicts it. release_lag above is unchanged: it still dates the point-in-time rows the panel is built from, so the panel's bytes do not move. This block governs only what a forecast may read, through repo_model.asof.

availability_provenance.note: Read on the human side and recorded 11 September 2026; it is a human-supplied reading and not something any code here fetched. The clause this replaces said the project has no network route to Treasury or the Board, which is no longer true of a job running natively on the user's machine -- the adapter added in A34 fetches the daily bill rates from there. The publication time itself is still read by a human and not by any code, which is what this object records. It replaces a release_lag note that recorded no publication time at all and said checking it was a human-side step.
availability_provenance.publication: Federal Reserve Statistical Release H.15, Selected Interest Rates: the daily bulk data file, published at 16:30 ET. The interactive H.15 page publishes at 16:15 ET, and the indicative closing quotations these rates are taken from are struck at about 15:30 ET.

coverage: bill rates by tenor, in percent
treasury_bill_rates.limitation: One field per tenor and quoting basis the Daily Treasury Bill Rates export carries, in percent as published. The tracked exports are one CSV per year, 2018 through 2026, and their header is not stable: 17 weeks first appears in 2022 and 6 weeks in 2025, so the adapter maps every column by its own file's header name and refuses a column that maps to no declared field. A tenor is blank before its first auction in the year it appears (8 weeks through 2018-10-15, 17 weeks through 2022-10-18, 6 weeks through 2025-02-14) and those dates carry no observation for it, not a zero; each of those cells is recorded in the build's quality report under absent_cells with reason blank, as runs of consecutive quote dates in the file's own order. A series therefore starts when its tenor does, and the 6-week and 17-week series are short. Every tracked year, 2026 included, has a snapshot manifest recording the export url the file was downloaded from and, as retrieved_at, the time of that download -- one fetch, 2026-09-14T00:28:15.251265+00:00, for all nine files -- which is a measurement of the retrieval and not the commit-time ceiling that stood in for it by decision (11 Sep) before these files were fetched. Two panel columns draw on this source, each the coupon equivalent in percent as published: tbill_4w from tbill_4w_coupon_equivalent and tbill_13w from tbill_13w_coupon_equivalent.

release_lag.note: The export carries one date per row, the quote date, and it is used as record_date. Availability is declared at 16:30 New York on that date, and the evidence for it is in availability_provenance beside this block rather than in this sentence. Which instant: 16:30 is the H.15 bulk data file, and the bulk file is what the adapter's shape corresponds to -- it reads Treasury's own whole-year CSV export, not an interactive page, so the earlier 16:15 interactive instant is not the one this source is read through, and 16:30 is in any case the later and therefore the conservative of the two. 15:30 is when the indicative closing quotations are taken, not when anyone outside Treasury could read them, and declaring it would be leakage with a citation attached. The previous declaration was end of day, asserting no publication time because none had been read; it is now established to have been conservative rather than early, because end of day is later than either publication instant. Moving it to 16:30 moves availability earlier, which is the only direction this declaration can cause harm, which is why the evidence is declared machine-readably and guarded by registry.check_availability_provenance rather than left in prose. At a 16:00 decision time -- the one every published run uses -- 16:30 and 23:59 both fall after it, so the purge this source contributes is unchanged.

fed_iorb_announcements.limitation: Not a panel column. src/repo_model/announced_iorb.py computes both fields per scored row from tests/fixtures/snapshots/fed-iorb-announcements/iorb_changes.csv, reading only the notes announced at or before that row's decision instant, and adds them to a panel in memory; the published panel does not carry them. The table holds every IOER/IORB implementation note that changed the rate from 2018-04 to its retrieval, plus the 2018-03-21 anchor and the 2021-07-28 note that replaced IOER by IORB at an unchanged rate. Announcement time is the FOMC statement's release time. Added by directive #38.

Stated for the registry's shape as treasury_auctions states it, at the end-of-day convention on the value's own date, the conservative direction. fed_iorb_announcements.reviewed_note: No structural zeros: a 0.0 change is a computed value, not a missing one.

scheduled_availability.evidence: Keyed on the announcement time. The value for scored date T is computed by repo_model.announced_iorb.announced_iorb_features from the implementation notes whose announcement instant (the FOMC statement's 'For release at' time, America/New_York) is at or before 16:00 on the panel day before T, so it is public at that instant by construction. Every row of tests/fixtures/snapshots/fed-iorb-announcements/iorb_changes.csv is read from the fetched federalreserve.gov pages by scripts/build_iorb_table.py (--check rebuilds it), and check_announcements refuses a row whose effective date is not after its announcement date. tests/test_announced_iorb.py perturbs every note announced after a decision instant and requires the features at that instant unchanged, and pins 2020-03-16: the Sunday 2020-03-15 17:00 EDT cut is not read by the 2020-03-13 decision.
scheduled_availability.note: 16:00 is the published records' decision time. A run at an earlier decision time is refused by the availability guard rather than read late; the features must then be recomputed at that time.
